## What it is

A repeat cross-sectional study in The Lancet Global Health compared HPV prevalence in girls aged 17 to 18 years who had probably missed South Africa's school-based programme (819 girls surveyed in 2019) with the first cohorts offered it (1,538 girls surveyed in 2023), and HPV-16 and HPV-18 prevalence fell from 21.6% to 3.2% (adjusted prevalence ratio 0.17, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.24). The programme gave two doses of the bivalent vaccine to Grade 4 girls and reached 87% coverage with at least one dose in its first year (Machalek et al., 2026). Among girls living with HIV the fall was from 29.4% to 4.4% (adjusted prevalence ratio 0.18, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.32), while HPV-31 and HPV-45 also declined, which is consistent with cross-protection (Machalek et al., 2026).

## Why it matters

The authors describe the first population-level evidence of impact for a two-dose programme in a setting with endemic HIV, with reductions similar to those from three-dose programmes in high-income countries. HPV-16 and HPV-18 prevalence was also 74% lower among unvaccinated girls in the 2023 cohort, which suggests indirect protection, and the authors name very high early coverage as a key factor (Machalek et al., 2026). That lesson matters for Zambia, where cervical cancer causes more than 3,000 new cases and over 1,900 deaths each year, while between 2019 and 2022 only 73% of girls aged 14 and 15 years received at least one dose and fewer than half of those eligible received a second (UNICEF Zambia, 2023). The September 2023 multi-age cohort campaign aimed to reach 1.42 million girls aged 9 to 14 years (UNICEF Zambia, 2023).

## What to remember

We should read the result as fewer infections, not yet fewer cancers, as the study measured prevalence in clinic attendees. Nearly all girls living with HIV in the 2023 sample were on antiretroviral therapy (294 of 295), so impact might be lower where treatment coverage is lower (Machalek et al., 2026). Few participants had received a single dose, which means the study does not test the single-dose schedule that WHO allows for girls aged 9 to 14 years, and WHO advises at least two doses, and three where possible, for people living with HIV (WHO, 2022).
